newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia Gazprom resumes normal Belarus gas supplies.
newsitem.headline: Russia Gazprom resumes normal Belarus gas supplies.

text.p: Russia resumed normal natural gas supplies to Belarus after an agreement was reached in Moscow on Tuesday on regulating payments of unpaid bills, a spokesman for Russian gas monopoly Gazprom said on Wednesday.
Supplies to Ukraine are still below normal, but a deal is possible later on Wednesday with Kiev, where Gazprom chairman Rem Vyakhirev is in talks with debtors, the spokesman added.
"Our supply to Belarus is back to the full volumes," said Sergei Smirnov. "We reached an agreement with the Belarussian side during talks in Moscow on Tuesday."
Gazprom met a Belarussian delegation, including Belarus's deputy prime minister in charge of fuel and energy, Valery Kokorev.

Gazprom had cut supplies to Belarus by a half earlier this week in response to late payments and resumed normal exports late on Tuesday. Exports via Belarus to Poland and Lithuania were not affected, Smirnov said.
He said Belarus had agreed to start paying off its arrears, pegged at $125.5 million, in August.
Gazprom said it expected to supply 16.6 billion cubic metres (bcm) of natural gas to Belarus in 1997.
Smirnov also said a deal with Ukraine, where Gazprom supplies have been cut by a third, could be reached by the end of the day.
"Our chairman Vyakhirev is in Kiev now and he leaves at the end of the day, so he will be looking to come to an agreement by then," Smirnov said.

Gazprom said on Tuesday supplies to Ukraine had been reduced by one third to 37-40 million cubic metres a day. Again exports to markets beyond Ukraine's borders were not affected. Russia originally intended to export 53 bcm to Ukraine in 1997.
The cuts to both countries are a sign that Gazprom is no longer willing to tolerate late payments among former Soviet republics.
The company is Russia's largest corporate tax payer, but had fallen behind on payments to federal coffers because domestic and foreign customers owed it vast sums in unpaid bills.
Moscow is putting pressure on its energy sector to contribute more money to the budget and Gazprom has recently transferred trillions of roubles in back taxes to the government.
